# Strict inverse-power radial rigidity and ordinary depth equality
not assert that a sampled mixed-integer radial law is convex, and it does
not resolve OC. The strict exponent and the dimension restriction below
are essential to the proof.

## 1. Setting and radial rigidity theorem

Let r>=2, let beta>r+1, and let f be a nonnegative integrable density on
R^r, with positive finite integral and full-dimensional convex positive
support U. Assume that the extended function g=f^(-1/beta), assigned
+infinity off the positive support, is convex. Fix y in int U. Boundary
values of f can be changed on the null boundary of U without affecting
any statement about its measure. Define the ordinary Ball radial body B
about y, translated to the origin, by

    rho_B(u)^r = r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(y+tu) dt.

The independently audited inverse-power Ball theorem proves that B is a
convex body with 0 in its interior. Write p_B for its Minkowski gauge:

    p_B(x)=inf{t>=0:x belongs to tB}.

**Theorem 1.** If B is a polytope, then, up to a Lebesgue null set,

    f(y+x)=F(p_B(x)).                                    (1)

Here there is R in (0,infinity] such that F is positive and continuous
on [0,R), zero for t>R, and F^(-1/beta) is convex and nondecreasing on
[0,R). In particular F is nonincreasing. Its normalization is

    r integral_0^R t^(r-1)F(t)dt=1.                     (2)

The support interior is y+int(RB), with the evident interpretation when
R=infinity. No symmetry of B or of f is assumed.

### Proof: equality on a facet forces equality of ray quantiles

Translate y to zero. The analytic bounds in the audited Ball lemma give
0<c<=g on U, a global integrable radial majorant, continuity of f on int U,
and positive finite radial integrals in every direction. For every
x in the boundary of B the ray integral I(x)=integral t^(r-1)f(tx)dt
is the same number 1/r. Multiply f by r in this paragraph, so those
integrals are one, and use the correspondingly rescaled g=(r f)^(-1/beta)
in the displayed quantile calculation. This multiplication does not affect
convexity or any equality argument. The profile F and normalization (2)
refer again to the original density after that calculation.

Choose distinct x_1,x_2 in one facet of B, and 0<lambda<1. Their convex
combination z lies in that same facet, so I(x_1)=I(x_2)=I(z)=1 in this
normalization. Let R_1(v),R_2(v), 0<v<1, be the increasing quantiles of
the probability densities t^(r-1)f(tx_1), t^(r-1)f(tx_2). They are C^1
and strictly increasing before their possibly infinite endpoints. Put

    T=(lambda/R_1+(1-lambda)/R_2)^(-1),
    a=lambda T/R_1,  b=(1-lambda)T/R_2,  a+b=1,
    X=g(R_1 x_1),   Y=g(R_2 x_2).

The exact quantile proof of the Ball theorem gives

    T^(r-1) f(Tz) T'
      >= T^r [a X^beta/R_1^r+b Y^beta/R_2^r]/(aX+bY)^beta
      >= T^r/[a R_1^s+b R_2^s]^(beta-1)
      >= 1,                                             (3)

where s=r/(beta-1) is STRICTLY between zero and one. The first step is
convexity of g, the second is weighted Holder, and the last is strict
concavity of the s-th power with T=aR_1+bR_2. Every quantity is positive.
If R_1(v)!=R_2(v) at any v, continuity makes the last inequality strict
on a nonempty interval of v. Integrating (3) over (0,1) then makes the
ray integral at z strictly exceed one: the change of variable T ranges
from zero to a value at most the endpoint of its ray, and any omitted
remaining ray mass is nonnegative. This contradicts I(z)=1. Therefore

    R_1(v)=R_2(v) for every 0<v<1.                       (4)

The two ray probability laws are identical. Their endpoints coincide,
and their densities t^(r-1)f(tx_i) coincide for almost every t>0. On the
common positive interval they are continuous, so f(tx_1)=f(tx_2) there
pointwise, including the value at t=0 by continuity at the origin.

All ray profiles on the boundary of one facet are therefore identical.
The facet-intersection graph of a full-dimensional polytope in r>=2 is
connected. Here is enough justification without a combinatorial theorem:
the boundary of B is homeomorphic by radial projection to the connected
sphere S^(r-1). If the finite facet-intersection graph had two components,
the corresponding unions of closed facets would be disjoint nonempty
closed sets partitioning that boundary, contradicting connectedness.
A common point of two meeting facets has a single ray profile. It follows
that all facets, and hence every point of the boundary of B, have one
common profile F. Their common endpoint is R in (0,infinity]. Every
nonzero point is t x with x in the boundary of B and t=p_B(tx), proving
(1) throughout the interior support, and zero off its closure. Values on
the support boundary are irrelevant, since a convex full-dimensional
support has a null boundary. The origin has its continuous profile value.

On any ray, h(t)=F(t)^(-1/beta) is convex for 0<=t<R. It is also
nondecreasing. Indeed, for 0<=s<t<R and x in the boundary of B, the point
sx lies in tB. Every point of the convex polytope tB is a convex
combination of its vertices. All those vertices have g-value h(t).
Convexity of g therefore gives h(s)<=h(t). This proves the claimed
profile properties. Finally the definition of B, applied to any one
boundary ray, is exactly (2). This completes the proof.

The same argument applies when the ray body is a convex body whose
boundary is a connected finite union of positive-dimensional flat faces.
Only the polytope case is used here. Nothing is claimed in dimension one:
facets then are isolated points and impose no equality between the two
ray laws. Nothing is inferred at beta=r+1: the exponent s in (3) is one,
so the strict equality argument is unavailable.

## 2. Minimal ordinary depth in the strict inverse-power class

For a density f of mass M, let

    D(f)=max_y inf_{closed halfspaces H containing y} integral_H f / M.

The audited inverse-power depth theorem proves that this maximum exists,
is attained in int U, and is at least Gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r. It also proves
that a deepest point y has finitely many active through-y caps whose
normals positively balance and hence whose union is all of R^r. These
facts hold for the strict class considered above as well.

**Theorem 2.** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, D(f)=Gamma_r if and only
if f is a gauge profile about the centroid of a simplex. More precisely,
there are a full-dimensional r-simplex T with centroid zero, a point y,
and a nonincreasing profile F with positive finite radial integral and
F^(-1/beta) convex on its positive interval, such that

    f(y+x)=F(p_T(x)) almost everywhere.                 (5)

The scale of T and of F is arbitrary; normalization (2) is required only
if T is taken to be the actual Ball radial body.

### Necessity

Let y be an attained deepest point with D(f)=Gamma_r. At y take the
finite active through-y cap cover just described. The ordinary Ball
body B preserves every through-y halfspace mass, so these same caps
have volume Gamma_r|B| on B and cover all of R^r. Every point of B is
therefore in a cap of that mass, which gives D(B)<=Gamma_r. Ordinary
Grunbaum gives the reverse inequality. The independently audited
ordinary minimum-maximal-depth rigidity theorem thus makes B a simplex.
The origin itself has depth Gamma_r in B, by preservation of all its
through-origin cap masses. A simplex has a unique deepest point, its
centroid: if any barycentric coordinate exceeds 1/(r+1), the corresponding
vertex cap has fraction strictly below Gamma_r. Thus B has centroid zero.
Theorem 1 supplies (5), with T=B and the claimed profile properties.

### Sufficiency

For any integrable gauge profile about any convex body T containing zero,
polar integration shows that every through-origin halfspace captures
exactly the same fraction of profile mass as it captures of |T|. The
common radial scalar cancels in the ratio. When T is a centroid-centered
simplex, ordinary Grunbaum gives depth Gamma_r at zero. Its r+1 canonical
vertex halfspaces through zero cover all of R^r, and each has profile
mass fraction Gamma_r by the same angular identity. Hence every possible
candidate point belongs to a cap with mass Gamma_r M and D(f)<=Gamma_r.
This proves equality. It also proves directly that (5) is sufficient
whenever the profile defines an integrable density; the convexity
hypothesis is needed for the necessity and for membership in the class.

## 3. Log-concave consequence

Every integrable log-concave density with full-dimensional support has
f^(-1/beta)=exp((-log f)/beta) convex for every beta>0, with the extended
value +infinity off its support. Taking any beta>r+1, Theorem 2 proves:
for r>=2 its maximal halfspace depth equals Gamma_r exactly when it is

    f(y+x)=exp(-h(p_T(x)))

for a centroid-centered simplex T and a convex nondecreasing function h
on an interval [0,R), with zero density outside that interval and with
positive finite integral. An additive constant in h changes only mass.
Here convexity and monotonicity of h follow from -log f exactly as in the
last paragraph of Theorem 1. Conversely these profile conditions imply
log-concavity, because a convex nondecreasing function of a convex gauge
is convex.

This includes constant density on a simplex, cone-profile marginals,
and exp(-p_T). It does not classify all borderline inverse-power
projective densities, and it does not identify any mixed-integer center.
